design_detail: Narrative review of the clinical pharmacology of methamphetamine: chemistry and molecular mechanisms; pharmacokinetics by route (Table 1) and detection times (Table 2); acute effects identified in prospective studies (Table 3); and adverse effects (overdose, psychosis, cardiovascular complications, withdrawal, neurotoxicity, neuropsychological impairment, Parkinson's disease, sexual behaviour, teratogenic and other effects). Literature from a PubMed search (English, human studies, 1966–2007), reference lists, book chapters and monographs; no inclusion criteria, no appraisal of the cited studies and no quantitative synthesis. 183 references.
can_establish: What the cited literature up to 2007 reported about methamphetamine's pharmacokinetics, acute effects and adverse effects, and which primary studies those statements come from, as a map of sources to read.
cannot_establish: How often any adverse effect occurs among people who use methamphetamine or among those who present with toxicity (the figures are second-hand and mostly lack denominators), what predicts death, or whether the chronic harms described are caused by methamphetamine (the cited observational studies are not appraised).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). PubMed search for methamphetamine, methylamphetamine or metamfetamine, limited to English-language human studies published 1966–2007: 447 articles, screened by hand; reference lists, book chapters and monographs from peak bodies added; inclusion decided by consensus between the two authors; mechanisms, chemistry and molecular pharmacology were not searched systematically (pp. 1085–1086, Methods).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded on screening: preclinical studies, review articles superseded by more recent reviews, and papers the authors judged less relevant (p. 1085). No inclusion criteria stated.
sample.selection_effects: Selection by the authors' judgment without stated criteria, from one database in English only. For acute toxicity the review relies on case reports (several of them amphetamine poisonings, from 1960 onward), a few emergency-department series and a treatment trial, and forensic series, which over-represent severe and fatal cases and give no population denominators.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The cited laboratory studies used low-to-moderate oral, intranasal, smoked or intravenous doses as study conditions, with one high-dose intravenous study of 12 people, for whom the review says previous histories of psychosis should be considered, without giving a number (p. 1088); illicit amounts come from self-report, which the review notes has not been substantiated objectively (p. 1088).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed for the toxicity and mortality evidence: the proportion of deaths with other drugs detected is not given.

comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed for the observational evidence on psychosis, cognition and Parkinson's disease, beyond previous psychosis among the high-dose study's participants (p. 1088) and family history of schizophrenia in persistent psychosis (p. 1091).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (they vary across the cited studies).
outcomes.operationalization: Overdose features are listed from case reports; frequencies of features in non-fatal presentations come from emergency-department series; causes of death come from case reports and forensic series.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, without appraisal. Pharmacokinetics (p. 1087, Table 1): terminal plasma half-life about 10 hours across routes, with substantial individual variability (9.1 h intravenous, 12 h smoked, 9.1 h oral, 11 h intranasal); bioavailability 67–90% smoked, 67% oral, 79% intranasal. Acute toxicity (pp. 1088, 1091): among non-fatal presentations, agitation in about 20%, suicidal ideation in 6–12%, acute psychosis in 7–12%, rhabdomyolysis in up to 14% and seizures in 3–4%; an estimated 94 000 US emergency-department visits associated with recent methamphetamine use in 2005; proposed toxic (200–5000 µg/l) and fatal (above 10 000 µg/l) plasma concentrations overlap with reported deaths (as low as 90 µg/l) and survival (9460 µg/l). Psychosis (p. 1091): of 170 Japanese people with methamphetamine psychosis, 59% recovered within 30 days, 41% had symptoms beyond a month and 28% beyond 6 months of abstinence. Cardiomyopathy: a 3.7-fold increased risk (p. 1091). Parkinson's disease (p. 1093): one retrospective case–control study of amphetamines, an eightfold risk with a mean of 27 years between exposure and onset.
analysis.selective_reporting: The cited studies are neither appraised nor described by design or size. The overdose section lists features without saying how often they occur; the emergency-department frequencies come without sample sizes. The Parkinson's disease argument rests on one case–control study of amphetamines and a dopamine-transporter threshold argument. The neurotoxicity section equates a baboon regimen with human illicit use by simple body-weight scaling, without an allometric or pharmacokinetic basis (p. 1092).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A broad summary of the literature to 2007, with pharmacokinetic values from controlled human studies and adverse-effect frequencies taken second-hand from small clinical series and case reports.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract links repeated use, through neurotoxicity, to prolonged psychiatric symptoms, cognitive impairment and an increased risk of Parkinson's disease (p. 1085); the body supports the Parkinson's link with one case–control study of amphetamines and an extrapolation from dopamine-transporter deficits that, by its own account, are below the level associated with Parkinsonian signs (p. 1093). The neurotoxicity section states as established that repeated exposure to amphetamines damages dopaminergic and serotonergic axons, mainly from animal work (p. 1092). The abstract does not mention the overdose syndrome. Within the toxicity section the statements are modest and follow the cited sources, but frequencies are given without denominators, and the forensic observation that many methamphetamine-related deaths result from accidents, suicide and homicide is not quantified.

timeline.event: This review: half-life about 10 hours; overdose features and frequencies from case reports, emergency-department and forensic series.
Review cites this review (its reference 16) for the methamphetamine half-life
Review gives about 10 hours for the methamphetamine half-life, citing this review

replication.where_it_stands: A widely reused reference review for pharmacokinetics. For acute toxicity it is a pointer to primary sources that are still to be read and carded before any frequency is cited: emergency-department series (Gray et al., 2007; Derlet et al., 1989), a treatment trial (Richards et al., 1997), case reports and forensic series of deaths (Inoue et al., 2006; Kalant and Kalant, 1975; Logan et al., 1998; Shaw, 1999; Zhu et al., 2000).

funding.funder: No funding statement for the review; the first author was supported by a Dora Lush Scholarship from the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia (p. 1094, Acknowledgements).
funding.affiliations_note: Pharmacology and Anaesthesiology Unit, University of Western Australia; Division of Mental Health, St George's, University of London (p. 1085). None of the authors' own studies is cited. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: For acute toxicity: prospective emergency-department or poison-centre cohorts of people presenting after methamphetamine use, with toxicological confirmation, recording how often each feature occurs, the case fatality and the features at presentation that predict death, with denominators. For the chronic harms, the primary cohort and case–control studies the review cites, appraised directly.

domains.note: A documented PubMed search (terms, limits, 447 hits) and reference-list searching, but selection by the authors' judgment of relevance without stated criteria, one database, English only, and no systematic search for mechanisms.

No appraisal: case reports, emergency-department series, a treatment trial and animal studies are cited side by side, frequencies without denominators; some qualifications are given (the high-dose study's participants, the concentration ranges, self-reported illicit amounts).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the authors' own studies is cited.
Mechanisms in Table 3 are labelled possible, but human neurotoxicity and the Parkinson's disease risk are stated with more confidence than the cited evidence carries.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on adverse effects (descriptions of severe cases against how often harms occur)
domains.note: The under-represented side is evidence on how often harms occur among people who use methamphetamine: the toxicity and chronic-harm sections rest on case reports and clinical samples. Recovery is mentioned (resolution of most psychoses, partial recovery of striatal markers with abstinence).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review documents a search but selects without criteria and does not appraise what it cites; it qualifies some evidence carefully but not its statements on human neurotoxicity and Parkinson's disease. It may be cited for pharmacokinetic summaries traced to their primary studies and as a pointer to the primary toxicity literature; frequencies of toxic features are to be cited from the primary series, and a claim resting on this review alone stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: Search: PubMed, English-language human studies 1966–2007, 447 articles screened by hand; preclinical studies, superseded reviews and papers judged less relevant were excluded; reference lists, books and monographs added; inclusion by consensus of the two authors; mechanisms not searched systematically.

The terminal plasma half-life of methamphetamine is about 10 hours, similar across routes but with substantial individual variability; Table 1 gives 9.1 h (intravenous), 12 h (smoked), 9.1 h (oral, range 3–17) and 11 h (intranasal).
key_findings.locator: Clinical pharmacology › Clinical pharmacokinetics, 3rd paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Table 1 values are mean ± standard error and/or range from single studies (references 33, 152, 153, 11, 30, 154, 32); see reporting issues on the intranasal row.

key_findings.finding: Based on case reports, the common features of methamphetamine overdose are agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension and rapid respiration; other features include shivering, dyspnoea, chest pain, hyperpyrexia and cardiac, hepatic or renal failure; coma and seizures are less frequent. An estimated 94 000 US emergency-department visits were associated with recent methamphetamine use in 2005.
key_findings.note: The sources for the features (references 29 and 44–51) are case reports, several of amphetamine poisoning, published from 1960 onward.

key_findings.finding: Non-fatal methamphetamine toxicity presents typically with tachycardia, hypertension and altered mental status: agitation in about 20% of cases, suicidal ideation in 6–12%, acute psychosis in 7–12%; rhabdomyolysis in up to 14% of presentations; seizures in 3–4%.
key_findings.note: No sample sizes or denominators are given. By the reference list, the sources are an evaluation of amphetamine-related emergency presentations (Gray et al., 2007), a trial of benzodiazepine against butyrophenone treatment of methamphetamine toxicity (Richards et al., 1997), 127 cases of amphetamine toxicity (Derlet et al., 1989) and a paper titled as a study of protection against d-amphetamine toxicity (Derlet et al., 1990), which may not be a clinical series; none has been read.

key_findings.finding: Case reports attribute methamphetamine-associated deaths most often to multiple congestion, pulmonary oedema or congestion, cerebrovascular haemorrhage, ventricular fibrillation, acute cardiac failure or hyperpyrexia, and others to septic injection or aspiration of vomit; several forensic studies suggest that a significant and possibly greater proportion of methamphetamine-related deaths arise from accidents, suicide and homicide.
key_findings.note: The causes of death rest on a single case report (Inoue et al., 2006) and a 1975 review of deaths in people who used amphetamines (Kalant and Kalant); the forensic series are from the USA, Taiwan and Japan (references 58–60). No proportions are given.

key_findings.finding: Proposed toxic (200–5000 µg/l) and fatal (above 10 000 µg/l) plasma concentrations are guides only: deaths have been reported at concentrations as low as 90 µg/l and survival at 9460 µg/l.
key_findings.locator: Adverse effects › Methamphetamine overdose, 4th paragraph (after Table 3)
key_findings.note: The PDF's text layer renders the unit µg/l as mg/l throughout; the printed pages show µg/l (checked on the rendered pp. 1087, 1088 and 1091).

key_findings.finding: Few systematic studies exist on cardiovascular complications, so most of the evidence comes from case studies: acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection and sudden cardiac death; a 3.7-fold increased risk of cardiomyopathy; and, from population studies, a higher risk of haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke.
Among 170 Japanese people with methamphetamine psychosis, 59% recovered within 30 days, 41% still had symptoms after a month and 28% after more than 6 months of abstinence.

The case for an increased Parkinson's disease risk rests on one retrospective case–control study (prolonged amphetamine use, an eightfold risk, a mean of 27 years between exposure and onset; reference 133), on the argument that Parkinsonian signs appear with striatal dopamine-transporter deficits of 47% or more, against 20–30% in people recently abstinent from methamphetamine, plus an age-related decline of about 4.5% per decade, and on one study (reference 105, Volkow et al., 2001) cited both for psychomotor dysfunction consistent with Parkinson's disease and for Parkinson-like disturbances in people whose dopaminergic damage was within the Parkinson range. The review also notes two studies (references 107 and 123: Johanson et al., 2006; Chang et al., 2002) that did not find such deficits despite neuronal pathology consistent with the disorder.

reporting_issues.issue: The review writes that dopamine-transporter deficits in recently abstinent people are typically 20–30% of normal levels, which taken literally means a 70–80% deficit; the argument (deficits below the 47% associated with Parkinsonian signs) requires reductions of 20–30%.
reporting_issues.consequence: A wording error that reverses the size of the deficit if quoted as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the intranasal half-life (11 ± 1 hours) carries footnote a, which the legend defines as a peak effect estimated from plots of subjective effect; and the intravenous time to peak concentration is printed as 6 ± 11 minutes, a standard error larger than the geometric mean it accompanies.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the footnote is misplaced or the half-life was read from a plot; the intravenous value cannot be interpreted as printed. Neither value is used in a claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the intranasal time to peak plasma concentration as 4 hours (reference 35), while Table 1 gives 169 ± 8 minutes (reference 32); the two sources are not reconciled.
In Table 3 the mechanism given for increased blood pressure reads as an increase in heart rate in pithed rats via α-adrenoceptors, apparently repeated from the heart-rate row.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor copy error in the mechanisms column.

reporting_issues.issue: Of the four sources cited for the features and frequencies of non-fatal presentations (references 52–55), two are titled as series of amphetamine-related presentations or amphetamine toxicity (Gray et al., 2007; Derlet et al., 1989), one as a study of protection against d-amphetamine toxicity (Derlet et al., 1990), which may not be a clinical series, and one as a treatment trial in methamphetamine toxicity (Richards et al., 1997).
reporting_issues.consequence: The frequencies may not describe people presenting with methamphetamine toxicity; to be checked in the primary papers before any is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says population studies indicate that methamphetamine raises the risk of haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke, citing references 50 and 78; reference 50 is a series of four cases and reference 78 is a population-based study of young adults hospitalized with amphetamine or cocaine diagnoses, so only one source is a population study and its exposure is not specific to methamphetamine. The 3.7-fold cardiomyopathy figure comes from a single study in young patients (reference 76).
reporting_issues.consequence: The stroke and cardiomyopathy statements (key finding 6) are stronger than their sources; reference 78 should be cited for stroke in people with amphetamine or cocaine diagnoses, not as methamphetamine-specific population evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The review's statement that a fatal overdose has been reported after a single intravenous dose rests on one case report (reference 29), whose title describes a patient who died nine days after the injection.
reporting_issues.consequence: A single case with nine days of survival cannot be read as describing typical fatal exposures; the review gives no population data linking dose to death.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says psychosis can occur at the higher doses typically used by people who use illicit methamphetamine, as a fact, while the body says the self-reported illicit amounts behind this have not been substantiated objectively and the pharmacokinetics of illicit methamphetamine remain to be described, adding only that forensic plasma levels are consistent with them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract is more certain than the body about what people who use illicit methamphetamine actually take; the body's caveat should accompany any use of the abstract's statement.

disagreements.first_pass: The case for an increased Parkinson's disease risk rests on one retrospective case–control study (prolonged amphetamine use, an eightfold risk, a mean of 27 years between exposure and onset) and on the argument that Parkinsonian signs appear with striatal dopamine-transporter deficits of 47% or more, against 20–30% in people recently abstinent from methamphetamine, plus an age-related decline of about 4.5% per decade.
disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10 (corrected): the paragraph also cites reference 105 (Volkow et al., 2001) both for psychomotor dysfunction consistent with Parkinson's disease and for Parkinson-like disturbances at damage in the Parkinson range, and references 107 and 123 that found no such deficits; the case rests on reference 133, the transporter-threshold and age-decline argument, and reference 105, with two contrary studies noted.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on p. 1093 and in the reference list (105 Volkow et al. 2001; 107 Johanson et al. 2006; 123 Chang et al. 2002; 133 Garwood et al. 2006). Rewrote the finding to add reference 105 and the two studies that found no deficits; the case-control, threshold and age-decline details are unchanged.

disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10 (card wording): the card says several of the high-dose study's participants had previous psychosis; the review says only that their previous histories of psychosis should be considered (p. 1088), without a number.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on p. 1088 (the sentence after the description of the 12 participants). Replaced the unsupported count word with what the review says.

disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10: the analysis field calls the concentrations blood concentrations; the review says plasma.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on p. 1091 (plasma concentrations; key finding 5 already says plasma). Terminology corrected.

disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10 (note): the values of this finding are printed on p. 1091, but the card's note cites only pp. 1087-1088 for the unit check.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed: the unit was checked on the rendered p. 1091 as well, where the proposed concentrations and the 90 and 9460 values are printed. Note extended.

disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10 (missed): stroke population studies (p. 1091, Cardiovascular complications, 3rd paragraph): references 50 (four cases, Perez et al., 1999) and 78 (population-based, hospitalized young adults with amphetamine or cocaine diagnoses, Westover et al., 2007); the 3.7-fold figure comes from one study (reference 76, Yeo et al., 2007).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed against p. 1091 and the reference list (50, 76, 78). Added as a reporting issue; key finding 6 reports the review's wording accurately and is left as it is.

disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10 (missed): fatal-overdose statement (p. 1091, 4th paragraph of the overdose section) rests on one case report (reference 29, Ago et al., 2006), titled as a death nine days after a single intravenous dose.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on p. 1091 and in reference 29's title. Added as a reporting issue without repeating the dose figure.

disagreements.reviewer: Reader 10 (missed): the abstract states the amounts typically used illicitly as fact, while the body notes that the self-reports behind them have not been substantiated objectively (p. 1088).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed: abstract (p. 1085) against the end of the pharmacokinetics section (pp. 1087-1088). Added as a reporting issue; no dose figures are repeated in the card.
